title: How disabled tests manifest in test maintainability challenges?
authors: Kim, D.; Yang, B.; Yang, J.; Chen, T.
venue: Proceedings of the 29th ACM Joint Meeting on European Software Engineering Conference and Symposium on the Foundations of Software Engineering (ESEC/FSE 2021)
supporting_sentence: Our life-cycle analysis shows that 41% of disabled tests are never brought back to evaluate software quality, and most disabled tests stay disabled for several years.
relevance: Only large-scale study of disabled-test prevalence and lifetime; direct precedent for a skip-ratio drift indicator in Java suites.

title: Are test smells really harmful? An empirical study
authors: Bavota, G.; Qusef, A.; Oliveto, R.; De Lucia, A.; Binkley, D.
venue: Empirical Software Engineering
supporting_sentence: The first study finds that there is a high diffusion of test smells in both open source and industrial software systems with 86 % of JUnit tests exhibiting at least one test smell and six tests having six distinct test smells.
relevance: Quantifies test-smell prevalence at 86% of JUnit tests; the benchmark any BDD drift-prevalence claim must be positioned against.

title: An empirical analysis of the distribution of unit test smells and their impact on software maintenance
authors: Bavota, G.; Qusef, A.; Oliveto, R.; De Lucia, A.; Binkley, D.
venue: 2012 28th IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance (ICSM)
supporting_sentence: The results show that (i) test smells are widely spread throughout the software systems studied and (ii) most of the test smells have a strong negative impact on the comprehensibility of test suites and production code.
relevance: First empirical distribution of test smells over 18 systems plus a controlled comprehension experiment; grounds prevalence-first drift measurement.

title: On the Relation of Test Smells to Software Code Quality
authors: Spadini, D.; Palomba, F.; Zaidman, A.; Bruntink, M.; Bacchelli, A.
venue: 2018 IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME)
supporting_sentence: we collect data on 221 releases of ten software systems and we analyze more than a million test cases to investigate the association of six test smells and their co-occurrence with software quality
relevance: Repeated-snapshot (221 releases) smell study relating smells to change and defect proneness; closest longitudinal design to ours.

title: The secret life of test smells - an empirical study on test smell evolution and maintenance
authors: Kim, D.; Chen, T.; Yang, J.
venue: Empirical Software Engineering
supporting_sentence: 1) Although the number of test smell instances increases, test smell density decreases as systems evolve.
relevance: Shows smell counts rise while smell density falls across 12 systems; warns that raw-count drift indicators can invert direction.

title: Paired Code Smells and Test Smells: A Fine-Grained Longitudinal Empirical Study
authors: Cai, Z.
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (PACMSE)
supporting_sentence: By analyzing 128,417 commits across 19 long-lived open-source Java repositories, we investigate the statistical associations, survival lifespans, and removal motivations of these paired flaws.
relevance: Git-mined survival analysis of test smells over 128,417 commits; proves longitudinal smell dating is feasible and already done.

title: On the diffusion of test smells and their relationship with test code quality of Java projects
authors: Martins, L.; Costa, H.; Machado, I.
venue: Journal of Software: Evolution and Process
supporting_sentence: We split the projects into three clusters to analyze the distribution of test smells, the co-occurrences among test smells, and the correlation of test smells and structural metrics of test code.
relevance: Largest test-smell dataset (13,703 Java projects); establishes cross-project prevalence baselines and smell co-occurrence that we must acknowledge.

title: Investigating Severity Thresholds for Test Smells
authors: Spadini, D.; Schvarcbacher, M.; Oprescu, A.; Bruntink, M.; Bacchelli, A.
venue: Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Mining Software Repositories (MSR 2020)
supporting_sentence: To accomplish this, we first analyzed some 1,500 open-source projects to elicit severity thresholds for commonly found test smells.
relevance: Shows smell-detection rules need severity thresholds; cautions against unweighted smell counts as drift signals.

title: Machine learning-based test smell detection
authors: Pontillo, V.; Amoroso d'Aragona, D.; Pecorelli, F.; Di Nucci, D.; Ferrucci, F.; Palomba, F.
venue: Empirical Software Engineering
supporting_sentence: The performance of the machine learning-based detector is significantly better than heuristic-based techniques, but none of the learners able to overcome an average F-Measure of 51%.
relevance: Demonstrates test-smell detection itself is unreliable (F-measure at most 51%), a direct threat to any smell-based drift indicator.

title: A Trend Analysis of Test Smells in Python Test Code Over Commit History
authors: Fushihara, Y.; Aman, H.; Amasaki, S.; Yokogawa, T.; Kawahara, M.
venue: 2023 49th Euromicro Conference on Software Engineering and Advanced Applications (SEAA)
supporting_sentence: most kinds of smells tend to increase over commits, i.e., many test smells are likely to have remained in test code as technical debt
relevance: Commit-history trend analysis of Python test smells across 100 projects; direct precedent for dating smell introduction via git.

title: Test Code Quality and Its Relation to Issue Handling Performance
authors: Athanasiou, D.; Nugroho, A.; Visser, J.; Zaidman, A.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
supporting_sentence: The results reveal a significant positive correlation between test code quality and two out of the three issue handling metrics (throughput and productivity), indicating that good test code quality positively influences issue handling performance.
relevance: Links a composite test-code-quality model to issue-handling outcomes; shows the field's outcome variables are maintenance metrics rather than mutation.

title: Understanding myths and realities of test-suite evolution
authors: Pinto, L.; Sinha, S.; Orso, A.
venue: Proceedings of the ACM SIGSOFT 20th International Symposium on the Foundations of Software Engineering (FSE 2012)
supporting_sentence: our findings show that test repair is just one possible reason for test-suite evolution, whereas most changes involve refactorings, deletions, and additions of test cases
relevance: First study of how unit test suites actually evolve; establishes refactoring and deletion as dominant, framing scenario removal as normal drift.

title: Understanding Test Deletion in Java Applications
authors: Bhatta, S.; Kendemah, F.; Jha, A.
venue: 2025 IEEE/ACM 22nd International Conference on Mining Software Repositories (MSR 2025)
supporting_sentence: we first create DelTest, a dataset of 24,431 manually confirmed deleted tests, by analyzing 449,592 commits from seven open-source Java projects
relevance: Quantifies test deletion at 24,431 tests and separates obsolete, redundant and failing ones; direct precedent for reading removed scenarios as drift.

title: Do System Test Cases Grow Old?
authors: Feldt, R.
venue: 2014 IEEE Seventh International Conference on Software Testing, Verification and Validation (ICST)
supporting_sentence: The test case half-life is between 5 to 12 months for the two studied data sets.
relevance: Introduces test-case activation curves, hazard curves and half-life (5-12 months); the only explicit survival model of test-case aging.

title: Rotten Green Tests
authors: Delplanque, J.; Ducasse, S.; Polito, G.; Black, A.; Etien, A.
venue: 2019 IEEE/ACM 41st International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE)
supporting_sentence: The results of the evaluation show that the tool is effective; it detected 294 tests as rotten-green tests that contain assertions that are not executed.
relevance: Defines rotten green tests, i.e. passing tests whose assertions never execute; the closest existing construct to assertion weakening.

title: Rotten green tests in Java, Pharo and Python: An empirical study
authors: Aranega, V.; Delplanque, J.; Martinez, M.; Black, A.; Ducasse, S.; Etien, A.
venue: Empirical Software Engineering
supporting_sentence: The presence of a rotten green test is a test smell, and a bad one, because the existence of a test gives us false confidence that the code under test is valid, when in fact that code may not have been tested at all.
relevance: Cross-language proof that assertion-less passing tests exist in Java and Python; validates vacuous-oracle drift as a real phenomenon.

title: How the Experience of Development Teams Relates to Assertion Density of Test Classes
authors: Catolino, G.; Palomba, F.; Zaidman, A.; Ferrucci, F.
venue: 2019 IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME)
supporting_sentence: we focus on how development teams' experience is associated with the assertion density, i.e., the number of assertions per test class KLOC, that has previously been shown as an effective way to decrease fault density
relevance: Establishes assertion density as a measurable test-quality indicator over 12 projects; supplies a reusable metric for assertion-thinning drift.

title: Studying Fine-Grained Co-evolution Patterns of Production and Test Code
authors: Marsavina, C.; Romano, D.; Zaidman, A.
venue: 2014 IEEE 14th International Working Conference on Source Code Analysis and Manipulation (SCAM)
supporting_sentence: The results show 6 co-evolution patterns and provide insights into their appearance along the history of the analyzed software systems.
relevance: Fine-grained association-rule co-evolution of production and test code over five systems; methodological template for pairing code churn with test churn.

title: Mining Software Repositories to Study Co-Evolution of Production & Test Code
authors: Zaidman, A.; Van Rompaey, B.; Demeyer, S.; van Deursen, A.
venue: 2008 IEEE International Conference on Software Testing, Verification and Validation (ICST)
supporting_sentence: In this paper we investigate whether production code and the accompanying tests co-evolve by exploring a project's versioning system, code coverage reports and size-metrics.
relevance: Founding co-evolution study using versioning plus coverage; supplies the churn-versus-coverage vocabulary our scenario-age indicator borrows.

title: Foundations for the study of software architecture
authors: Perry, D.; Wolf, A.
venue: ACM SIGSOFT Software Engineering Notes
supporting_sentence: PARAPHRASE: Perry and Wolf separate architectural erosion (violations of the architecture) from architectural drift (insensitivity about the architecture) as the two causes of a system's increasing resistance to change; the PDF text layer is OCR-degraded so no clean verbatim span is quotable.
relevance: Origin of the erosion versus drift distinction in SE; the vocabulary our construct must inherit rather than reinvent.

title: A multiple case study of design pattern decay, grime, and rot in evolving software systems
authors: Izurieta, C.; Bieman, J.
venue: Software Quality Journal
supporting_sentence: We found no evidence of design pattern rot in these systems. However, we found considerable evidence of pattern decay due to grime.
relevance: Defines and longitudinally measures design-pattern decay, grime and rot; a vocabulary precedent for graded rather than binary degradation.

title: Assessing architectural drift in commercial software development: a case study
authors: Rosik, J.; Le Gear, A.; Buckley, J.; Babar, M.; Connolly, D.
venue: Software: Practice and Experience
supporting_sentence: However, implementations often diverge from their intended architectures: a phenomenon called architectural drift.
relevance: Establishes drift as divergence between an intended and an implemented artefact; exactly the relation we posit between the scenario and step layers.

title: Assessing architectural evolution: a case study
authors: Wermelinger, M.; Yu, Y.; Lozano, A.; Capiluppi, A.
venue: Empirical Software Engineering
supporting_sentence: This paper proposes to use a historical perspective on generic laws, principles, and guidelines, like Lehman's software evolution laws and Martin's design principles, in order to achieve a multi-faceted process and structural assessment of a system's architectural evolution.
relevance: Operationalises Lehman's evolution laws as measurable historical drift metrics; the model for turning evolution laws into indicators.

title: On the Interplay Between Software Testing and Evolution and its Effect on Program Comprehension
authors: Moonen, L.; van Deursen, A.; Zaidman, A.; Bruntink, M.
venue: Software Evolution (Springer)
supporting_sentence: as tests ease software evolution by offering a safety net against unwanted change, they can equally be experienced as a burden because they are subject to the very same forces of software evolution themselves
relevance: Explicitly states tests are subject to the same evolution forces as code; the conceptual warrant for a test-side drift construct.

title: Test smells 20 years later: detectability validity and reliability
authors: Panichella, A.; Panichella, S.; Fraser, G.; Sawant, A.; Hellendoorn, V.
venue: Empirical Software Engineering
supporting_sentence: the older tool's detection strategies misclassified over 70% of test smells, both missing real instances (false negatives) and marking many smell-free tests as smelly (false positives)
relevance: Shows the test-smell vocabulary mismatches real concerns and detection misclassifies over 70%; a decisive caution against smell-count drift indicators.

title: Lightweight Assessment of Test-Case Effectiveness Using Source-Code-Quality Indicators
authors: Grano, G.; Palomba, F.; Gall, H.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
supporting_sentence: The key results of the study reveal that our estimation model only based on static features has 86 percent of both F-Measure and AUC-ROC.
relevance: Closest prior work relating static quality indicators to mutation score, but at individual test-case level and cross-sectional only.

title: Test code refactoring unveiled: where and how does it affect test code quality and effectiveness?
authors: Martins, L.; Pontillo, V.; Costa, H.; Ferrucci, F.; Palomba, F.; Machado, I.
venue: Empirical Software Engineering
supporting_sentence: we will measure how refactoring operations impact the quality and effectiveness of test code
relevance: Registered report behind the EMSE 2024 paper; nearest planned link from test-quality indicators and smells to mutation coverage.
